1793.title: Thermal Equilibrium
1793.heading: Thermal Equilibrium
1793.content: Two systems are in thermal equilibrium when no net heat transfer occurs between them. They then have the same temperature, even if their materials or stored internal energies differ. The zeroth law makes this relation transitive and permits a thermometer in equilibrium with a system to represent its temperature.

1799.heading: Thermal Equilibrium and Temperature Difference
1799.content:
A temperature difference is the driving force for conduction, convection, and radiation. Net transfer diminishes as temperatures equalize, and thermal equilibrium is reached when no temperature difference remains to sustain spontaneous heat flow.

Thermal equilibrium alone is narrower than thermodynamic equilibrium. The broader condition also requires mechanical and chemical equilibrium, so no unbalanced internal force, reaction, or matter redistribution remains alongside the absence of net heat transfer.

1802.title: Thermal Diffusivity from Material Properties
1802.heading: Thermal Diffusivity from Material Properties
1802.content:
Thermal diffusivity is the ratio of thermal conductivity to density times specific heat capacity, $\alpha=k/(\rho c_p)$. It characterizes how rapidly a temperature disturbance spreads through a material relative to the material's capacity to store energy.

Because it is derived from three other properties, a thermal model can compute it rather than require it as an independent input. Laser-flash analysis can measure its temperature dependence by heating one face of a specimen and tracking the opposite face's transient response.

1805.title: Thermal Convection
1805.heading: Thermal Convection
1805.content:
Thermal convection transfers energy between a solid surface and a surrounding fluid. The heat-flow rate is proportional to surface area, heat-transfer coefficient, and the difference between surface and ambient temperature.

In a finite element model, convection contributes both a coefficient to the thermal matrix and an ambient-temperature term to the load vector. It is a boundary condition rather than volumetric conduction.

1808.heading: Thermal Boundary Layer
1808.content:
Near a solid wall, fluid temperature changes from the surface value toward the bulk-flow value across a finite region. This thermal boundary layer concentrates temperature gradients and therefore strongly influences convective heat flux.

Wall orientation, buoyancy, roughness, and imposed velocity alter the layer and the effective [[Convective Heat Transfer Coefficient|heat-transfer coefficient]]. A numerical mesh must resolve this near-wall variation finely enough that further [[Thermal Mesh Refinement|refinement]] does not materially change the reported flux.

A thermal boundary condition specifies how a model exchanges energy with its surroundings. Common forms prescribe temperature, heat flux, convection to an ambient, radiation, insulation, symmetry, or continuity across an interface.

Each condition acts on selected geometric entities and must match the physical boundary being represented. An omitted or misapplied condition changes the energy balance, while mutually inconsistent conditions can make the finite-element problem overconstrained or physically meaningless.

1814.title: ThemeRiver
1814.heading: ThemeRiver
1814.content: A ThemeRiver is a flowing stacked-area display whose combined thickness is centered symmetrically around the horizontal axis. The total width shows the global sum, while colored bands show the components' changing contributions. Centering creates a visually balanced shape but removes the stable baseline already missing from most internal layers of a [[Stacked Area Time-Series Plot]]. It favors broad patterns and relationships over exact component values.

1817.title: Thermal Analysis
1817.heading: Thermal Analysis
1817.content:
Thermal analysis determines temperature distribution and derived heat flow in a body. In the primer, it is a scalar finite element problem because each node carries one temperature degree of freedom.

The procedure selects an element and temperature interpolation, derives conduction and source terms, assembles the global equations, applies thermal boundary conditions, and solves temperatures before recovering gradients and heat fluxes.

Texture Paint mode applies color directly to an image while the artist paints on the corresponding 3D mesh. A usable UV layout connects each brush stroke on the model to a location in the flat texture.

Painting on the model is effective for blocking color and placing detail in context. The image and UV guide can later be moved to a dedicated two-dimensional graphics program when more specialized painting tools are needed.

Blender's Texture Paint workspace keeps the 3D Viewport and Image Editor connected to the same canvas. Brush, blend, stroke, texture, mask, falloff, symmetry, and slot settings determine how a stroke is generated and where its pixels are written.

1895.heading: Text Tokenization
1895.content:
Text tokenization divides a document into units that an analytical system can process, commonly using whitespace and punctuation to approximate words. The resulting tokens become the observations used for counts, vectors, searches, or classification.

Token boundaries are analytical choices rather than neutral facts. Punctuation, compound forms, and domain-specific expressions can carry meaning, so a tokenizer should be selected and validated for the corpus.

1898.title: Text Representation
1898.heading: Text Representation
1898.content:
Text representation retains selected information from a document as features suitable for search, classification, clustering, recommendation, or prediction. Every representation emphasizes a perspective: character strings preserve surface form, bags of words preserve term occurrence, and structural or latent models preserve other relationships.

The representation should map text objects relevant to the same task into similar descriptions while separating objects that should differ. Richer representations can capture more meaning but often require more computation, data, and language-specific processing.

1901.title: Text Normalization
1901.heading: Text Normalization
1901.content:
Text normalization converts written forms into the words a speech synthesizer should pronounce. It expands abbreviations, numbers, dates, currencies, and symbols according to their context.

The same characters can require different readings, so simple character substitution is insufficient. Normalized text becomes input to [[Phonetic Transcription]] in a [[Text-to-Speech]] pipeline.

A testing pyramid layers many fast, narrow automated checks beneath fewer slow, broad playthroughs. Build configuration checks, unit and asset validation, smoke tests, level loads, automated playthroughs, and human QA provide progressively wider evidence.

Lower tiers run more frequently and block bad builds early. Higher tiers remain necessary because integrated game behavior and player experience cannot be inferred from component tests alone.

1937.title: Test-Driven Development
1937.heading: Test-Driven Development
1937.content:
Test-driven development creates an automated test before the functionality that will satisfy it, then implements the smallest behavior needed and improves the design under the test's protection. The test makes the intended behavior explicit before code structure dominates the decision.

The growing suite becomes a safety net for refactoring and change. TDD is most applicable to behavior that can be expressed reliably in automated checks.

ASP.NET Core and Angular tests apply the same cycle with different tools: xUnit.net and Moq isolate back-end behavior, while Jasmine, Karma, and TestBed exercise front-end components. [[Behavior-Driven Development]] provides a related emphasis on describing observable behavior.

The inventory project uses tests around commands, factories, and the shared repository to make expected behavior visible while the design changes. In particular, tests expose a race in concurrent quantity updates and a lifetime error when each resolution builds a new dependency-injection provider. Passing tests measure the implemented behavior, not the completeness of user acceptance testing.

1940.title: Test Suite
1940.heading: Test Suite
1940.content:
A test suite is a named collection of related tests that share a subject or behavior. Setup can be run before each test so every specification begins from a fresh and predictable fixture.

Jasmine uses descriptive suite blocks to group Angular expectations. Running the whole suite reveals whether a change preserved behavior across all included cases rather than only the test currently being edited.

1943.title: Test Spy
1943.heading: Test Spy
1943.content:
A test spy observes calls made to a function or service method and can optionally replace its result. It lets a test verify interaction without using the real dependency behavior.

An Angular component test can spy on a data-service method, return controlled values, and then assert how the component responds. The spy is one form of [[Test Double]].

1946.title: Test Double
1946.heading: Test Double
1946.content:
A test double is a substitute used in place of a production collaborator during a test. Fakes, stubs, mocks, and spies provide different kinds of controlled behavior or observation.

Replacing an HTTP service or database dependency reduces external variability and lets a [[Unit Test]] concentrate on one component. The chosen double should implement only the behavior relevant to that test.

1949.title: Test Fixture
1949.heading: Test Fixture
1949.content:
A test fixture is the prepared environment and state used to exercise a unit. It includes the subject, its configured dependencies, and any data needed before the action occurs.

In Angular testing, a component fixture gives the test access to both the component instance and its rendered element. TestBed creates that environment from a testing module configuration.

1952.title: Test Error
1952.heading: Test Error
1952.content:
Test error measures prediction mistakes on observations not used to fit the model. When the [[Test Dataset]] represents the intended prediction population and has remained untouched, it estimates generalization performance.

Using test results repeatedly to tune a model makes the test set part of development and biases the estimate. Cross-validation can guide model selection while preserving a final independent evaluation.

The book separates validation-guided development from a final test evaluation. This protects the reported error from the many choices made while comparing trees, random forests, boosting models, and thresholds.

1955.title: Test Dataset
1955.heading: Test Dataset
1955.content:
A test dataset is a collection of examples withheld from machine-learning training and used afterward to evaluate performance on unseen data. It checks whether behavior learned from the [[Training Dataset]] transfers beyond the examples used to adjust parameters.

Strong training performance paired with weak test performance is evidence of [[Overfitting]]. Because the model must not learn from the test answers during fitting, the test collection functions as an independent check rather than another training epoch.

The source uses held-out tissue samples to estimate misclassification error after a prediction rule has been trained. A sample cannot provide an honest test if its label or feature pattern was used to choose the fitted parameters being evaluated.

The book reserves the test partition for evaluation after model structure, tuning choices, and thresholds have been settled with training and validation data. This sequencing protects the final estimate from development feedback.

1973.title: Temporal Zooming
1973.heading: Temporal Zooming
1973.content: Temporal zooming narrows an [[Interactive Time-Series Plot]] to a selected interval and rescales the view to expose local variation. It allows a long series to provide both overview and detail without a separate figure for every period. The control should make the active interval visible and provide a reliable reset. Zooming changes what is shown, so comparisons made at different zoom levels must account for altered scales and context.

1976.title: Temporal Registration
1976.heading: Temporal Registration
1976.content:
Temporal registration aligns measurements, simulation state, rendering, and display output to compatible moments in time. Without it, correctly calibrated virtual geometry can lag behind a moving camera or object and appear spatially misplaced.

Timestamps help synchronize sensors with different rates, while prediction can estimate the pose expected when the generated image reaches the display. Variable or unknown latency makes this compensation more difficult.

1979.title: Temporal Polyline
1979.heading: Temporal Polyline
1979.content: A temporal polyline connects successive observations in a scatterplot according to their time order. The path shows how a pair of variables evolves, revealing direction, loops, reversals, and distinct trajectories that an unconnected point cloud conceals. Color can identify groups, and selected year labels can establish direction. Dense crossings remain difficult to follow, so [[Year-Panel Comparison]] or animation may complement the static path.

1982.title: Temporal Network
1982.heading: Temporal Network
1982.content:
A temporal network represents a changing graph as discrete time-indexed layers. Each layer is a snapshot, and interlayer connections associate entities that persist between adjacent times.

Keeping snapshots separate preserves when edges existed and allows communities or diffusion to be followed through time. Aggregating them into one graph can create paths that never existed at any single moment.

1991.content: Temporal color encoding maps observation time or a time-derived category to color. In a [[Time-Series Scatterplot Matrix]], it can reveal whether an apparent relationship belongs to a season, year, or transition. Ordered periods call for an ordered palette, while recurring categories such as months may require a cyclic or carefully arranged palette. Color supplements position but should not carry distinctions too numerous or subtle to discriminate reliably.

1997.heading: Temperature-Dependent Thermophysical Properties
1997.content:
Density, conductivity, heat capacity, viscosity, and emissivity may change over the temperature range traversed by a model. Replacing those relationships with constants can hide feedback between the evolving temperature and the coefficients governing its evolution.

Tables, interpolation functions, or analytic functions can represent measured dependence. The added nonlinearity may make convergence harder, so the model should compare the variable-property result with a justified constant-property baseline and inspect [[Thermal Model Uncertainty from Input Properties|input uncertainty]].

Interpolation tables or analytic functions should cover the simulated range and define deliberate extrapolation behavior. In a pipe, changing viscosity and density also changes Reynolds number, linking material data to [[Laminar Flow Selection for Thermal Models|flow-regime selection]].

2003.heading: Temperature Readings versus Intervals
2003.content: An absolute temperature reading on the Fahrenheit scale requires both an offset and a scale change to become Celsius: Pryor's example uses $T_{\mathrm C}=(T_{\mathrm F}-32)/1.8$, taking 50 °F to 10 °C. A temperature difference does not need the 32-degree offset; an interval of 18 °F corresponds to 10 °C. The book also notes that one kelvin interval and one Celsius-degree interval are equal in size. Applying a multiplicative interval factor to an absolute reading therefore gives a wrong result. See [[Reciprocal Conversion Factors]].

2012.title: Telerobotics
2012.heading: Telerobotics
2012.content:
Telerobotics is the remote operation of a robot that is geographically separated from its user. Because robots act in the physical world and can have many [[Degrees of Freedom]], their control often benefits from a [[3D User Interface]].

The interface must map the user's input to remote movement and return sufficient feedback for safe, accurate control. [[Latency]], incomplete sensory information, and mismatches between the user's controls and the robot's capabilities can make the task harder.

2015.title: Telepresence
2015.heading: Telepresence
2015.content:
Telepresence allows people in different physical locations to share task space and person space through an interactive system.

In a [[Virtual Environment]], remote users can appear and act in the same three-dimensional space even though their physical spaces differ. A telepresence interface must communicate who is present, where they are, and what they are doing while supporting social cues and coordination.

The concept connects [[Social Computing]], [[Computer-Supported Cooperative Work]], and [[Presence]].

Collaborative AR can create telepresence by placing a remote participant's video, avatar, annotations, or gestures into the local task space. In an asymmetric arrangement, a stationary expert may inspect a remote user's live view and return spatial guidance that appears registered with the user's physical environment.

2018.title: Technology Jumping
2018.heading: Technology Jumping
2018.content:
Technology jumping occurs when an industry moves from a maturing technology to a new one that can sustain rapid improvement. Successive waves—from punched cards to vacuum tubes, transistors, and silicon—can preserve an overall growth trend even when each substrate reaches limits.

Organizations watch for the inflection point where the current technology slows and a competitor’s alternative accelerates. The jump requires investment and redesign because new physical mechanisms often demand new architectures and skills.

2021.heading: Technology Adoption S-Curves
2021.content:
A technology adoption curve often begins with accelerating growth, reaches an inflection point, and slows as performance or market penetration approaches saturation. Plotted over time, this pattern resembles an S.

Business strategy must distinguish growth within the current curve from a jump to a new curve. Extrapolating early exponential growth indefinitely ignores physical, economic, and social limits.

2024.title: Technological Singularity
2024.heading: Technological Singularity
2024.content:
The technological singularity is a projected point after which accelerating machine intelligence makes social and technological change radically difficult to predict. In AI narratives, an [[Intelligence Explosion]] often drives the transition and produces [[Superintelligence]].

The term marks a limit of prediction rather than a detailed account of what follows. It can support utopian expectations of abundance and human enhancement or catastrophic expectations of loss of control. Because these futures are highly speculative, they should be distinguished from ethical problems created by systems that already classify, recommend, monitor, or decide.

2027.title: Technological Dependence
2027.heading: Technological Dependence
2027.content:
Technological dependence occurs when ordinary life, institutions, or critical services become difficult to maintain without a technical system. Dependence can create convenience and capability while converting the system's weaknesses into human vulnerabilities.

With AI, dependence may reduce the knowledge and practical ability needed to check or replace automated judgments. It also increases the consequences of error, attack, or loss of access. Ethical deployment therefore considers fallback procedures, human competence, and resilience rather than measuring only normal performance. A system that works efficiently but leaves no safe alternative can make its users less autonomous.

2030.title: Technological Mediation
2030.heading: Technological Mediation
2030.content:
Technological mediation is the way a technology helps shape how people perceive the world, choose actions, and relate to others. An AI system is not merely a neutral object between a user and a goal; its classifications, recommendations, and interface make some interpretations and actions easier than others.

Because mediation changes both experience and practice, ethics should enter during design rather than only after harm occurs. The relevant unit is the relationship among people, technology, and context. This view connects [[Posthumanism]] with [[Ethics by Design]] while preserving attention to the power built into concrete systems.

2033.title: Technical Replicate
2033.heading: Technical Replicate
2033.content:
A technical replicate repeats measurement of the same biological material to characterize variability introduced by preparation, instruments, or measurement procedures. It does not represent an independently sampled biological unit.

Comparing technical with [[Biological Replicate|biological replicates]] helps separate measurement noise from genuine variation among organisms or specimens. Treating technical replicates as independent biological samples would overstate the effective sample size.

2036.title: Technical Confounding
2036.heading: Technical Confounding
2036.content:
Technical confounding occurs when a processing variable is associated with the biological outcome of interest, making their effects difficult or impossible to distinguish. A gene-expression difference attributed to population, treatment, or sex may instead reflect processing date or batch.

When the alignment is perfect, no statistical adjustment can recover the separate effects from that dataset. Randomizing biological groups across batches prevents the design failure more reliably than post hoc correction.

2039.content:
Team resource visibility means that collaborators share a realistic understanding of available time, skills, tools, money, and attention. A design decision made without those constraints merely postpones the conflict until implementation.

Making capacity explicit supports informed tradeoffs and fair commitments. It also allows the team to reduce scope or change a prototype before hidden overload becomes missed work or resentment.

2042.title: Team Coaching
2042.heading: Team Coaching
2042.content:
Team coaching helps a group understand its goals, relationships, practices, and impediments so it can solve its own problems. The coach supplies observation, questions, facilitation, and process knowledge without taking ownership of every solution.

Coaching aims to increase the team's capacity for reflection and self-management. It cannot repair structural conditions that the organization refuses to change.

2045.content:
Team dependency management makes cross-team needs visible, identifies when they must be satisfied, and gives both sides responsibility for coordination. Dependencies can be represented on shared boards and discussed before they block a Sprint Goal.

The first response is to reduce the dependency through team design, shared skills, or a thinner feature split. Scheduling a handoff manages the remaining cost but does not remove it.

2048.title: Team Communication Overhead
2048.heading: Team Communication Overhead
2048.content:
Team communication overhead grows faster than headcount because the number of possible person-to-person channels is n(n−1)/2. Adding people therefore creates coordination cost as well as capacity.

Large projects preserve shorter communication paths by organizing small teams around coherent outcomes and using explicit coordination mechanisms between them. More people do not automatically make a late or entangled effort faster.
